The whole report in 3 lines

  1. Who we are: a calm family money book. Not a MoMo copy: no payments, no loans, no paywalled history.
  2. What looks cheap: the layout is fine. Too much blue and loud estimates make it look like a template.
  3. What to do: 4 weeks, one theme each: Calm → Clear answer → Trust → Family. See the plan.
How to read this page: sections 1–4 are decisions and tasks. From "Why the calendar looks app-like" down is evidence. Open it only when you need a reason.

Where MyFinance fits: fix what the big apps get wrong

Short answer

Don't compete with MoMo on features. MoMo moves money, sells loans and fills its home screen. Money Lover locks your own history behind a paywall. Their unhappy users are asking for the opposite: a quiet, trustworthy money book that a family shares, where nothing is hidden, nothing is locked and nothing is sold to you. S16S17

  1. Money Lover's #1 complaint is "you locked my history". 43% of its 1–2★ reviews are about premium walls. Many people say they have to pay about 500k ₫ to see records they typed in themselves. S17
  2. Updates that rewrite your data are #2. 21% of complaints are about version 8.0, which force-merged categories and dropped budgets, and 13% are about data lost after a logout or a failed sync. S17
  3. MoMo's pain is fees, surprise charges and noise. 21% of its 1–2★ reviews mention fees or pay-later (ví trả sau) charges. Users also can't find their own auto-payments (Spotify, iCloud) and say the app has forgotten its core job. S16
  4. Families are underserved. A couple sharing Money Lover can't see "who spent how much". Your own calendar is full of family money: Ba đi đám cưới, Cho mẹ, Tiền trọ. S17S13
  5. MyFinance today is single-user. Every spending row belongs to one user_id. There is no household, no "paid by", no export and no gold or cash wallets yet. S18 VERIFIED

Six promises MyFinance can make

1 · Your history is yours

Never locked, never paywalled. Export everything to CSV/JSON at any time. Directly answers Money Lover's top complaint (43%).

2 · Updates never touch your data

No forced merges of categories or budgets. New features are opt-in. Migrations add, never rewrite.

3 · Built for a family

One shared book, a "paid by" on every item, private items when needed, and a monthly "who spent what".

4 · A watchdog, not a wallet

MyFinance never moves money, so it can't overcharge. It lists every subscription and auto-debit, and reminds you before pay-later and bill due dates.

5 · Vietnamese money as it really is

Cash, gold (vàng), money for parents and family events (đám cưới, hiếu hỉ), rent. Moving money between your own wallets is not spending.

6 · Calm and private

No ads, no upsell pop-ups, no loans. Opens fast. A privacy mode blurs amounts when someone looks at your screen.
How design fits in: the premium-design work in the rest of this report is how these promises feel. Calm colours, fewer borders and one clear number say "nothing here is trying to sell you something". INFERRED (positioning judgement)

What to do next: a 4-week plan

One theme per week. Do the tasks top to bottom; each has a time estimate and a "done when" check. INFERRED (times are estimates from reading the code, not measured)

Do not build: bank sync, payments, AI chat, loans. Those are what users of the big apps complain about.
  1. Week 1 · Calm · ~5–6 h (promise 6)
    • ☐ 15 min: grey estimates (change 1), the Start here task
    • ☐ 1 h: /mock the calendar in 3 palettes (navy like Copilot, ink + jade like Dash.fi, warm white like Monarch). Pick one.
    • ☐ 1 h: spend bar instead of blue fill (change 2)
    • ☐ 2–3 h: semantic colour tokens (change 3)
    • ☐ 30 min: tinted darks (change 4)
    Done when: the calendar uses at most 3 non-grey colours, each with one meaning.
  2. Week 2 · One clear answer · ~2 days (promise 4)
    • ☐ 2 h: "Safe to spend today" as the big number at the top of the sidebar. The value already exists: 142.836 ₫ a day for 27 days S14
    • ☐ 1 day: "Coming up · next 7 days" strip: plans, payday, subscriptions, bill and pay-later due dates (like Rocket Money)
    • ☐ 3 h: turn the "Spending evenly…" sentence into a small pace chart
    Done when: "how much can I spend today, and what's due this week?" takes under 2 seconds to answer.
  3. Week 3 · Trust · ~2–3 days (promises 1 and 2)
    • ☐ 1 day: Export everything (CSV for spreadsheets, JSON for full backup)
    • ☐ 1 day: "Import from CSV" for people leaving Money Lover
    • ☐ 2 h: privacy toggle that blurs amounts
    • ☐ 30 min: "Our promises" paragraph in Profile: no ads, no paywalled history, updates never rewrite your data
    Done when: a new user gets all their data out in one tap.
  4. Week 4 · Family v1 · ~3–4 days (promise 3)
    • ☐ 1 h: /mock the family screens first
    • ☐ 1 day: households + household_members tables; add household_id, paid_by, private to spendings and plans
    • ☐ 1 day: invite one person by link
    • ☐ 1 day: "paid by" on each item + monthly "who spent what" split
    Done when: two phones see the same calendar and each item shows who paid. INFERRED (schema sketch; today rows only have user_id S18)
  5. Later · Vietnamese money (promise 5): cash and gold holdings, savings pots, transfers between your own wallets that are not spending, a family obligations view (weddings, funerals, money for parents), goals with progress, "cover overspending" like YNAB.
How to know it worked: after week 4, use it with one family member for a full pay cycle. Success is (a) neither of you asks "who paid for this?", (b) nothing due in the cycle surprised you, and (c) you never felt the app wanted something from you.

Why the calendar looks "app-like", not "private bank"

Evidence starts here. You don't need anything below to do the plan. Come back when you want the reason behind a change.
Short answer

The layout is sound. What breaks the premium feel is visual noise: one saturated blue does five different jobs, every future day repeats the same blue italic dashed estimate, and the dark surfaces are neutral grey-black. Award-winning finance apps do the opposite. They show a summary first, keep colour for meaning, and let the numbers carry the design. S2S3S6

  1. Blue means too many things. In the screenshot, blue marks past-day spending (heat fill), planned estimates, today's border, "Left after plans", the add button and the active segment. var(--primary) appears 143 times across src/styles. S9S10S13 VERIFIED
  2. The future is louder than the past. 20 of the 30 cycle days show ~50.000 ₫ or ~130.000 ₫ in bold italic blue with dashed boxes. The repeated estimates take more visual weight than the real spending. S11S13 VERIFIED
  3. The heat fill turns real days into solid blue slabs. In dark mode the fill reaches 60% opacity of rgb(96,165,250), so 7 Nov reads as a button, not as data. S10 VERIFIED
  4. Premium apps tint their darks and mute their accents. Copilot never uses pure black and tints surfaces navy. Mercury avoids "loud blues for trust". MyFinance uses neutral zinc #09090b / #18181b with Tailwind's default #3b82f6. S2S3S9
  5. The fixes are mostly CSS and tokens. The top five changes touch globals.css, CalendarView.css and lib/heatmap.ts, with no change to data or layout. See the ranked plan. INFERRED (effort estimated from reading the files, not from building it)

Six things premium finance apps do

Across the benchmarks the same six habits repeat. None of them needs new features; they are decisions about what not to show loudly.

Colour only carries meaning

Dash.fi uses "three colours, three meanings": up, down and flat. It caps charts at five series. S6 YNAB names colours by role, so a balance colour means "negative", not "red". S5 Mercury keeps the whole palette muted on purpose. S3 The rule: if a colour does not mean something, make it grey.

Dark mode is tinted, not black

Copilot "never uses pure black" and tints every dark surface with deep navy. Its text sits at about 90% white, not 100%. S2 Copilot's own release notes list "Refreshed dark mode with higher contrast, easier-to-read text and softer borders". S1 Pure neutral greys read as "developer tool". A slight hue reads as "brand". INFERRED (design judgement, not measured)

Numbers are the typography

Mercury gives balances and amounts their own type style: 28px, weight 500. S3 Dash.fi requires font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums on every money column so digits line up. S6 Premium apps use medium weights and size for hierarchy. They avoid bold everywhere and avoid italics on numbers.

Summary first, detail on demand

Copilot: "The dashboard shows a summary first. No spreadsheet grids on launch". S2 Monarch is praised for "simple charts that make it easy to spot trends". S4 Detail is one tap away, not on screen all at once.

Forecasts look quieter than facts

A forecast is less certain than a real transaction, so it should look lighter. MyFinance's comment says the same thing: estimates should "never read as real". S11 But today the estimates are bold, italic and saturated, so they read louder than the real ones. Premium apps usually draw projections as thin, grey or hatched shapes. INFERRED (general pattern; we did not inspect each app's forecast screen)

Calm over clever

Copilot's own promotion describes "a design focused on clarity, control, and calm". S7 Mercury uses a roomy 1.625 line height. S3 Calm comes from fewer borders, more space and slower, smaller motion.

MyFinance next to the benchmarks

MyFinance already does several premium things: tabular numbers in the calendar, a clear "Left after plans" headline, and a runway bar. The gaps are in colour, the dark palette and the weight of forecasts.

Where the screenshot loses the premium feel

Four spots in the current calendar do most of the damage. Each is small in code.

Solid blue past days

getHeatmapColor fills a day with blue from 20% to 60% opacity in dark mode, scaled by that day's spending against the month's peak. S10 On 5–8 Nov the result is four bright slabs, the loudest thing on the page. White text on a 60% blue fill also looks like a selected state, not data. INFERRED (visual reading of the screenshot)

Estimates shout

Planned rows get font-style: italic, a dashed primary border and primary-blue amounts. S11 Repeated on 20 days, the dashed boxes form a grid pattern that the eye reads before the real numbers. The day totals (~50.000 ₫) are also larger than the real line items.

Neutral black plus default Tailwind blue

The base tokens are Tailwind's zinc greys and blue-500. S9 They are clean but generic, and many template dashboards share them. Copilot and Mercury avoid both: tinted darks and a muted accent. S2S3

Empty and filler states take full-size cards

"No expenses" weekends and the greyed days of neighbouring periods each get a full card with a border. S13 This adds 35 bordered boxes on one screen. Premium apps use fewer borders and let spacing separate items. INFERRED (design judgement)

What this research did not cover

  • OPEN We did not install the benchmark apps. The screenshots are the apps' own App Store marketing images, which are polished and may differ from the live app.
  • OPEN Vietnamese premium apps (Cake, Timo, MoMo's spending views) were not reviewed for design; no reliable design source was found in this pass.
  • OPEN Complaint shares come from the 500 most recent reviews per app on the Vietnamese App Store only (not Google Play), counted by keyword matching. Treat them as direction, not as precise numbers.
  • OPEN Is the family the first audience (you and relatives), or other families too? That decides whether week 4 needs invite links and a privacy model, or just two accounts on one household.
  • OPEN Brand colour choice (step 5) is a taste decision for you. A /mock page with 3 palette options would settle it.
  • OPEN Light mode was not assessed; the screenshot is dark mode only.
